contentMarkdown:
Job portals, university applications, and government forms love one specific number: 200KB. Your photo is 2MB, the upload field refuses anything bigger, and now you need to hit an exact target — not just "smaller." Hitting a target size isn't luck; it's one repeatable trick: lower the compression quality while watching the live file size, and stop when it dips under your target. JPEG quality settings map to roughly predictable size ranges, but the exact number differs from photo to photo — which is why watching a live size preview beats guessing a magic quality number.

## The fastest method: quality slider + live size preview

No software to install and no account to create — your browser does the whole job and the file never leaves your device.

1. Open the [free image compressor](/tools/image-compressor).
2. Drop in your JPG (it also accepts PNG, WebP, and GIF).
3. Drag the quality slider down — start around 70–75 for a first try.
4. Watch the live size preview update in real time.
5. Keep lowering the slider until the preview reads just under 200KB, then download.

Aim for 195–199KB rather than exactly 200, so rounding differences can't push you back over the limit. Because the compression happens locally in your browser, the preview shows the exact output size — what you see is exactly what you'll upload, and there's no upload wait even for large photos.

## If the slider alone won't get you under 200KB

Some images need one extra step. Try these in order:

**Lower the quality a bit more.** Photos usually stay visually fine down to about 60%. Below roughly 50% you'll start seeing blocky artifacts around edges and text, so don't go further unless the form forces you to.

**Switch the output format to JPG.** If you uploaded a PNG, the quality slider doesn't apply to it — PNG is lossless, so there's no quality dial to turn. Choose JPG as the output format and the slider starts working, often cutting a photo PNG to a fraction of its size. One honest caveat: JPG can't keep transparency, so if your image needs a transparent background, this route isn't for it.

**Shrink the dimensions.** Fewer pixels means a smaller file, guaranteed. Use the [free image resizer](/tools/image-resizer) to bring a 4000-pixel photo down to 1200–1600 pixels wide before compressing. Forms and portals display your photo at thumbnail size anyway — the extra pixels were only ever dead weight.

Combining a modest resize with 70% quality gets almost any photo under 200KB while still looking clean.

## When 200KB is the wrong target

Not every image should be squeezed to 200KB:

- **You need transparency** (logos, icons, overlays)? Stay with PNG. A 200KB JPG will flatten transparent areas into a solid color — usually white.
- **You're printing the photo?** Keep the original. 200KB is a screen-and-form size, not a print size.
- **Screenshots with lots of text?** Text degrades faster than photos at low quality settings. Stop around 70–75 and resize the dimensions instead of pushing the slider lower.
- **The original is already tiny?** An already-compressed 150KB photo can't shrink much further, and that's true of every compressor — the tool shows you the percentage saved honestly, even when it's near zero.

## The honest limits

Two things no compressor can promise: it can't tell you a single quality number that lands every photo at 200KB (every photo compresses differently), and it can't shrink an already-optimized file much further. What makes the target reachable is the live size preview — you adjust, you watch the real number, and you stop when it lands. Keep your original photo somewhere safe: you can always compress again, but you can't restore quality you've thrown away.

faqs.q: How do I compress a JPG to exactly 200KB?

faqs.a: For on-screen viewing and form uploads, usually not visibly. A quality setting around 70–80 typically cuts a photo's size by more than half with no visible difference. Below roughly 50% you'll start noticing blocky artifacts, so stop there unless the form leaves you no choice.
faqs.q: Will my photo look bad at 200KB?

faqs.a: PNG is a lossless format, so the quality slider doesn't apply to it. Switch the output format to JPG in the compressor, and the slider starts working — a photo PNG usually shrinks to a fraction of its size. If it still won't fit, resize the image to fewer pixels first.
faqs.q: My PNG won't compress below 200KB — what do I do?

faqs.a: Yes. JPG is the most widely accepted format for photo uploads on forms and portals, and compression only changes the file size, not the image content. Keep your original photo saved somewhere in case a form later asks for a higher-resolution version.
